extracted.intended_audience: researchers, scientometricians, and funding-agency staff interested in validating peer review and measuring research impact
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and empirical-summary for designing and interpreting studies that test whether pre‑funding peer review decisions predict later research impact; includes recommended impact indicators, study design controls, and cautions about metric limitations and bias. Intended to inform research-evaluation and policy work on grant peer review validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use multiple impact indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: Including a panel of indicators is likely to give a clearer picture of impact (Hicks et al., 2015).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Combine bibliometric and non-bibliometric measures (e.g., publications, citations, patents, funding success, faculty positions, career satisfaction, project initiation/completion, collaboration, spin-offs). Only 25% of surveyed studies used more than one indicator; relying on a single measure (especially bibliometrics) is common but insufficient. Different indicators may show different predictive validity, so use a set to improve robustness (examples: Melin & Danell found funded applicants published in higher-quality journals and received more external funding even when counts were similar).

rubrics_metrics.name: Balance comprehensiveness and feasibility when choosing indicators
rubrics_metrics.description: “The right balance between comprehensiveness and feasibility must be struck” when determining how many and what type of indicators to include.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select indicators appropriate to the research program and funding goals; avoid overly labor-intensive approaches for assessment of individual projects. Consider resource constraints when deciding whether to use comprehensive frameworks (e.g., Payback) or a smaller panel of feasible measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate quantitative and qualitative evidence in context
rubrics_metrics.description: Integration of information within a specific research context is crucial to getting an accurate picture of impact; holistic frameworks should involve qualitative and quantitative aspects as well as peer and end-user evaluation (Donovan, 2007).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret indicator panels against the scientific area, program goals, and implementation of peer review. Include stakeholder and end-user input where relevant and contextualize findings rather than relying on raw counts alone.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use established comprehensive frameworks when appropriate (Payback example)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Payback framework gauges “not just outputs but also outcomes derived from over a decade of investment” and accounts for impact latency and multiple sources of attribution.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Payback integrates knowledge creation, benefits to future research, political, health sector and economic benefits. It is suggested as best practice for broad research-evaluation, but is labor-intensive and may be less appropriate for assessing single projects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for latency and attribution of impact
rubrics_metrics.description: Impact often has delayed effects and multiple contributing sources; evaluations should account for latency and attribution to multiple sources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose time windows appropriate to the type of impact measured (bibliometric studies in this review had a median maximum impact measurement time of ~5 years). Recognize that different indicators manifest over different time horizons (e.g., patents, policy uptake, career outcomes).

rubrics_metrics.name: Include unfunded (rejected) control groups and pre‑funding (ex‑ante) controls
rubrics_metrics.description: Studies need access to funding decisions or peer review scores and their relationship to external outputs; having unfunded controls and ex‑ante performance data is important to isolate reviewer decision effects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Without unfunded controls, assessing whether funding itself (vs. selection) drives later outcomes is impossible. Compare ex-post outcomes while adjusting for ex-ante qualifications to de-couple funding effects from selection effects (many studies showed effects diminished after adjusting for ex-ante qualifications).

rubrics_metrics.name: Control for ex‑ante applicant/project quality
rubrics_metrics.description: When examining ex-post performance, studies should compare or adjust for ex-ante performance to remove the effect of pre-existing differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to control for ex-ante quality leads to misattribution of funding effects. Examples: Pion & Cordray, Bornmann et al. Many studies found funded applicants had higher pre-application productivity, complicating causal claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be cautious using citation-per-dollar or similar normalized metrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Citation level per dollar spent can mask correlations between peer review scores and bibliometric impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some studies using citation/$ found no predictive validity, possibly because normalizing by dollars obscures relationships. Consider alternative normalizations and be explicit about what a per-dollar metric implies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate time window for measuring impact
rubrics_metrics.description: The time window when impact is measured is an important variable — especially for bibliometric impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Median maximum time in bibliometric studies was ~5 years; results differed for ≤5 years vs. >5 years. Short windows may miss delayed impacts; very long windows may introduce other confounders. Choose and justify the window according to the field and impact type.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplement bibliometrics with non‑bibliometric measures
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric measures are most used but have many issues as accurate indicators of impact; social impact and non-bibliometric methods are needed (Bornmann, 2013).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider patents, technology transfer, clinical trial/guideline citations (for clinical research), surveys of usage, career outcomes, policy influence, reproducibility metrics (r-factor), post-project peer review, and collaboration measures. Use altmetrics and ALMs cautiously and comparatively (Dinsmore et al., Didegah et al.).

rubrics_metrics.name: Prioritize field-appropriate citation measures for translational/clinical research
rubrics_metrics.description: Traditional citation analysis may underestimate the impact of clinical research; prioritize citations from clinical trials or clinical guidelines to highlight translational impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Adjust bibliometric approaches to the normative citation behavior of the field; use domain-specific outcome measures where available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Measure reproducibility where feasible
rubrics_metrics.description: Given the importance of reproducibility, assessments of reproducibility (e.g., the r-factor) are relevant impact indicators.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include reproducibility checks or indicators in validation studies where applicable; note such measures are still under development but can be valuable complements to productivity metrics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Integrate and weight indicators thoughtfully
rubrics_metrics.description: Just as reviewers weigh review criteria, how one weighs the importance of each indicator into the overall picture of impact is of crucial importance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions about weighting should reflect program goals and scientific context. Report how indicators are aggregated and perform sensitivity checks to weighting choices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Address randomness, inequality, anomalies, and extreme events in interpretations
rubrics_metrics.description: Most evaluations fail to take into account “inequality, random chance, anomalies, the right to make mistakes, unpredictability and a high significance of extreme events” which distort measurements of impact (Bornmann, 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret indicators in light of high variance and the possibility of outliers; use robust statistics and consider distributional properties rather than just means.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider effect of impact assessment on incentives and peer review behavior
rubrics_metrics.description: The effect such impact assessment has on funding incentives is non-trivial and likely influences ex‑ante peer review decisions (Lindner & Nakamura, 2015; Bornmann, 2017).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that the use of certain metrics can change applicant and reviewer behavior; account for this when designing evaluation and when interpreting validation results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Test internal validity of the review process (bias, inter‑rater reliability, structures)
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a need to look at internal validity with examinations of potential reviewer bias, review structures and baselines of decision making; many studies indicate low inter‑rater reliability and reviewer-dependence of scores.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate inter-rater reliability, reviewer effects, panel processes (teleconference vs face-to-face), and potential biases. Internal tests of fairness, efficiency, and rationality are crucial complements to outcome-based validation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid analyses that exclude relevant score ranges without justification
rubrics_metrics.description: When poorer‑scoring unfunded applicants or projects are excluded, observed validity can disappear; exclusion decisions affect conclusions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include the full score range or justify exclusions; perform analyses stratified by score bands to see where discrimination holds (coarse discrimination between poor and better proposals vs. finer discrimination among top applicants).

rubrics_metrics.name: Negotiate access to pre‑funding peer review data
rubrics_metrics.description: Improved access to pre-funding peer review data is necessary; academics should work with funders to gain access and funders should invest in validation studies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Data sharing agreements between researchers and funding agencies are recommended to enable robust validation studies; advocate for infrastructure/policies that permit anonymized data sharing for research.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match evaluation design to program-specific goals and context
rubrics_metrics.description: Different research programs have different goals which may include both bibliometric and non-bibliometric outcomes; these should be observed to give context.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Customize indicator panels, time windows, and weighting to the specific funding mechanism, target population (e.g., early-career), and programmatic objectives. Be cautious about generalizing across agencies and mechanisms.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be mindful of the Matthew effect and differential returns to funding
rubrics_metrics.description: Interpretations should account for the Matthew effect — funding historically advantaged groups may behave differently and funding less-awarded groups may achieve higher impact.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider subgroup analyses (e.g., early-career vs established) and alternative hypotheses that selection for high ex-ante performers may not maximize later impact. Use designs that can detect differential treatment effects across groups.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer multiple-study or mixed‑method approaches to validate peer review
rubrics_metrics.description: Many studies are single-indicator or single-method; mixed and multi-indicator studies provide a more comprehensive and valid test.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use bibliometrics, surveys, patent/licensing data, post-project peer review, and qualitative case studies in combination. Triangulate findings across methods to strengthen inferences about validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report limitations and variability explicitly
rubrics_metrics.description: Bibliometric measures show large variability which can obfuscate correlations or firm conclusions; interpretation is sometimes made difficult due to potential effect of funding itself.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explicitly report limitations, sample sizes, control availability, and sensitivity analyses. Acknowledge when observed differences are small and when causality cannot be established.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider portfolio-level decisions and complementary funding mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: Because some meritorious research will not be funded and discovery is partly unpredictable, funding administrators should incorporate portfolio diversification, programmatic concerns, collaboration promotion and risk considerations into final decisions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use peer review validation studies to inform but not wholly determine allocation; complement peer review with program-level policies (e.g., early-career funds) and diversified funding strategies to maintain a healthy research ecosystem.
